clinicalPearls: Postmenopausal bleeding is the cardinal presenting symptom and must be investigated to exclude malignancy in every woman
The commonest type is endometrioid adenocarcinoma, which is oestrogen-driven and associated with obesity, nulliparity, late menopause, and unopposed oestrogen exposure
Serous and clear cell carcinomas are less common, oestrogen-independent, tend to occur in older women, and behave more aggressively
Endometrial thickness on transvaginal ultrasound helps triage postmenopausal bleeding, but a normal measurement does not exclude the aggressive non-endometrioid subtypes
Diagnosis rests on endometrial sampling by pipelle biopsy or hysteroscopy with directed biopsy, particularly when bleeding persists despite a thin endometrium
Most cases are diagnosed early because bleeding prompts presentation, and total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is the mainstay of treatment
Lynch syndrome should be considered, especially in younger women, and molecular classification increasingly guides adjuvant therapy and prognosis
Tamoxifen use, polycystic ovary syndrome, and diabetes are additional risk factors reflecting chronic unopposed oestrogen and metabolic influences
reference.pathophysiology: Type 1 (endometrioid) tumours develop through prolonged oestrogenic stimulation of the endometrium unopposed by progesterone, progressing through endometrial hyperplasia with atypia to invasive carcinoma; they commonly harbour PTEN, PIK3CA, and mismatch repair defects. Type 2 (serous and clear cell) tumours arise in atrophic endometrium independent of oestrogen, frequently carry TP53 mutations, and are more likely to invade deeply and metastasise early. Spread occurs by myometrial invasion, transtubal and peritoneal dissemination, and lymphatic routes to pelvic and para-aortic nodes.
additionalDifferentials: Endometrial hyperplasia with or without atypia
additionalInvestigations: Transvaginal ultrasound to measure endometrial thickness and assess the myometrium
Endometrial biopsy (pipelle) or hysteroscopy with directed sampling
Histopathology with grade, subtype and molecular classification
Pelvic MRI to assess depth of myometrial invasion and cervical involvement
CT chest, abdomen and pelvis for staging in high-risk histology
Mismatch repair immunohistochemistry and testing for Lynch syndrome
redFlags: Postmenopausal bleeding, which requires prompt investigation to exclude cancer
Recurrent or persistent bleeding despite a reassuring initial ultrasound
Aggressive serous or clear cell histology with deep myometrial invasion
Evidence of nodal or distant metastatic spread on imaging
Pyometra or haematometra in an elderly woman suggesting obstructing tumour
reference.prognosis: The majority of women present with disease confined to the uterus and have an excellent prognosis after surgery, but outcome worsens with deep myometrial invasion, high tumour grade, aggressive histological subtypes, and nodal or distant spread. Molecular subgroups, notably POLE-mutated tumours with favourable and p53-abnormal tumours with adverse outcomes, are refining prognostic estimates and adjuvant treatment decisions.
pitfalls: Failing to investigate postmenopausal bleeding because it is light or intermittent
Relying on a thin endometrial stripe to exclude aggressive non-endometrioid tumours
Attributing bleeding to atrophy or polyps without histological confirmation
Missing Lynch syndrome by not testing younger patients or those with a suggestive family history
Overlooking an oestrogen-secreting ovarian tumour as an underlying cause
